text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which forces the right side of the heart to work harder and leads to symptoms as the heart and lungs struggle to get enough oxygen-rich blood to the body.
snippet_highlighted_words: the heart and lungs struggle to get enough oxygen-rich blood to the body

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages of PAH, you may not notice any symptoms at all. When initial signs do appear, they often develop slowly over months or years and are easy to confuse with other heart or lung conditions:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical exertion like walking up stairs or exercising.
Lightheadedness or dizziness, particularly when active.
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat).

text_blocks.snippet: As the disease progresses and places more strain on the heart, symptoms can become more severe or occur even while resting:

list.snippet: Edema (swelling in the ankles, legs, feet, or lower abdomen/neck due to fluid retention).
Fainting spells (syncope) or severe dizziness during exertion.
Cyanosis (bluish or grayish tint to the lips, fingers, or skin from low oxygen levels).
Bloated abdomen or unexplained weight gain from fluid buildup.
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness in rare, advanced cases where enlarged arteries press on chest nerves.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about recognizing and managing these signs through resources like the American Lung Association Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Guide.
